question.prompt: In 'The spare seat', why does the new player ask Anika to play slowly?

options.text: so he can follow the opening

question.explanation: He explicitly asks her to play the opening slowly so he can follow. The request is for help learning the music, rather than a judgement about her instrument.

stimulus.title: The spare seat
stimulus.body:
At the first rehearsal, Anika chose a chair in the back row. From there she could watch the violin bows without anyone watching hers. When the conductor asked for a volunteer to play the opening phrase, she bent to retie a perfectly secure shoelace.

On Thursday a new player arrived carrying a battered case. The only empty chair stood beside Anika. He opened his music upside down, noticed, and laughed. 'I hoped nobody would see that,' he said. Anika showed him where to begin.

During the break he asked her to play the opening slowly so he could follow. She played it twice, stumbling once. He thanked her anyway. After the break, the conductor asked again for a volunteer. Anika's hand moved before she had time to study her shoelace.

Her first note trembled. From the chair beside her came a small, steady tap of a shoe keeping time. The rest of the phrase followed. Afterwards, she left her music on the chair while she fetched water. She was saving the seat, but no longer hiding in it.

workedSolution: He explicitly asks her to play the opening slowly so he can follow.
The request is for help learning the music, rather than a judgement about her instrument.

Review originality, vocabulary, difficulty and time for an above-average Year 5/6 learner.

question.prompt: At noon in 'A cooler courtyard', what was the temperature difference between the surfaces in degrees?
question.explanation: The mat read 34 degrees and the paving 28 degrees at noon. Subtract 28 from 34 to obtain six degrees; the starting reading is not used for this comparison.

stimulus.title: A cooler courtyard
stimulus.body:
The following account describes a fictional school investigation. Students wanted to know whether two courtyard surfaces warmed differently in sunlight. They placed identical thermometers on a dark rubber mat and pale paving at 10 am. Both surfaces began at 19 degrees. At noon the mat read 34 degrees and the paving 28 degrees. At 2 pm a cloud covered the courtyard; both readings fell.

One pupil proposed replacing every dark surface immediately. The teacher asked whether one afternoon could settle the decision. The mat lay near a warm wall, while the paving was exposed to a light breeze. The students had measured temperature on the surfaces, not the air where people walked.

For a second trial they planned to exchange the thermometers, measure several days and choose locations equally sheltered from wind. They would also compare the cost and durability of possible replacements. Their first results were useful: they provided a reason to investigate further. They did not yet provide a complete purchasing plan.
